in_context.text: Paul has just told Philemon to put anything Onesimus owes on Paul's account. Here he signs that promise in his own hand: "I will repay it." Then he gently adds that Philemon owes Paul "even thine own self besides."

speaker.text: Paul, a prisoner of Jesus Christ, writing with Timothy. He stresses that he writes this line personally: "I Paul."

audience.text: Philemon, a beloved fellow-worker of Paul, in whose house a church met.

affected.text: Onesimus, Philemon's servant, who had left him and became a believer through Paul. Any debt or wrong of his is what Paul offers to cover.

what.text: Paul makes a signed pledge to pay whatever Onesimus owes Philemon. He then reminds Philemon, without pressing it, that Philemon is in Paul's debt for something greater: his own self.

events.text: Paul writes while in prison, after Onesimus became a believer through him, and as he sends Onesimus back to Philemon.

written.text: Traditional view: about AD 60-62, from Rome, at the same time as Colossians. Scholarly view: nearly all accept Paul wrote it, but some place the imprisonment at Ephesus (about AD 54-55) or Caesarea (about AD 57-59).

where.text: Paul writes from prison; the letter does not name the city, and Rome is the traditional view. It was sent to Philemon, traditionally at Colossae, which the letter itself does not name.

purpose.text: Paul removes any money obstacle to Philemon welcoming Onesimus back. By taking the debt on himself, he makes it easier for Philemon to receive Onesimus "as myself."

big_picture.text: Paul appeals for love's sake rather than commanding, and he takes another's debt on himself. The aside about what Philemon owes echoes Paul's words elsewhere about those who came to faith through him: "in Christ Jesus I have begotten you through the gospel" and "are not ye my work in the Lord?" The verse itself does not spell out the debt.

for_readers.text: The verse shows love that pays the cost of reconciliation. Paul does not just ask Philemon to forgive; he offers to carry the loss himself.

why_it_matters.text: The lexicon links "with my own hand" to Paul's personal signatures in 1 Corinthians 16:21, Colossians 4:18 and 2 Thessalonians 3:17. Here, writing in his own hand backs his promise, "I will repay it."
The word means "to pay off, repay," and the lexicon lists Philemon 19 as its New Testament use. It is the language of settling an account, matching "put that on mine account" in verse 18.
The word means "to owe besides or still." Paul is saying that, beyond any debt Onesimus has, Philemon still owes Paul something more: his own self.

takeaway.text: Paul puts his own name and money behind Onesimus's welcome home. He reminds Philemon gently that he owes Paul "even thine own self besides."

resolved.reason: Calls Onesimus a "runaway" servant, but the sources only say he "departed" and "had left" Philemon; they do not say he ran away.
resolved.fix: claim rewritten to match its sources

resolved.reason: Galatians 6:11 only says Paul wrote with his own hand; it is not a signed pledge or financial guarantee, so "as also in Galatians 6:11" goes beyond the cited text.
